title: Split Rivals into Two Teams
statement:
n people, numbered 1 to n, must be split into two teams. Each pair [a, b] in rivals says that a and b refuse to be on the same team. A team may be empty, and people with no rivals can go anywhere.

Return true if everyone can be placed so that no two rivals share a team, and false otherwise.

examples.why: Teams {1, 4} and {2, 3}. Every rival pair is split.
1 and 2 are easy, but 3, 4 and 5 are all rivals of each other, and three people cannot be split pairwise over two teams. Every group has to be checked, not just the first one.
Going around the ring of five, teams must alternate A, B, A, B, A, and then 5 and 1 are both on A. Any odd ring fails, not only triangles.

hints: Draw people as nodes and rivalries as edges. Once you put one person on team A, what do you know about their rivals?
Every placement is forced once you pick a team for one person in each connected group. Spread the colour with BFS or DFS and look for a conflict.
A conflict means two rivals got the same colour. That happens exactly when the group contains a loop of odd length. Remember to start a new search for every group that is still uncoloured.

explain.intuition:
This is graph two-colouring. Put person 1 on team A. Their rivals must be on B, the rivals' rivals on A, and so on. Inside one connected group there is no choice at all, so just propagate the colours and check that no edge ends up with the same colour on both sides.

The only way to fail is an odd loop of rivalries: walking around it the colours alternate, and an odd length brings you back to the start with the wrong colour. Groups that are not connected are independent, so each needs its own starting point. Forgetting that is the usual bug.
steps: Keep color[p], initially unset. For each person with no colour, give them colour 0 and start a BFS.
For each person u taken from the queue and each rival v: if v has no colour, give it 1 − color[u] and queue it; if it has the same colour as u, return false.
If every BFS finishes cleanly, return true.
pitfalls: Starting the search only from person 1. A bad group elsewhere, like the triangle in the second example, is never seen.
Building a one-way adjacency list. A rivalry goes both ways.
Indexing people from 0 when the input numbers them from 1.

solutions.title: Two-colour with BFS
solutions.idea: Colour each uncoloured person 0, then spread alternating colours along rivalries. A rival with the same colour means it cannot be done.

solutions.title: Union-find on the rivals
solutions.idea: All rivals of one person must share a team, so union them together. If a person ever ends up in the same set as one of their rivals, it fails.

followups: If a split exists, return the two teams. If not, return one odd loop of rivals as proof.
Rivalries arrive one at a time. Report the first one that makes a split impossible. (Hint: union-find with parity.)
